analysis.one_liner: Matches small campaign donations with public funds so House candidates can win without big donors.
analysis.headline: The Government by the People Act was referred to three House committees in May 2024, drew 4 cosponsors, and died there without a markup or a vote when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a voluntary public financing system for House campaigns. Candidates who show real grassroots support—1,000 small donors giving at least $50,000 total—could receive public matching payments worth 6 times each donation of $200 or less, plus a larger payment before general elections. It would also give every eligible adult in three pilot states a $25 voucher to give to House candidates. The program would be paid for entirely by a 4.75% surcharge added to federal fines, penalties, and corporate settlements—no general taxpayer money.
analysis.who_benefits: First, candidates who can raise money from many small donors but lack access to large donors: they would get public matching funds worth 6 times each small contribution, making a $25 donation worth $150 to the candidate [S2]. Second, ordinary voters: smaller donors would count for more in House races, and in three pilot states every resident would get a $25 voucher they can direct to any House candidate [S2]. Candidates who join the program must cap donations from any individual at $1,000, use no personal funds above $50,000, and drop joint fundraising committees and leadership PACs, which reduces the leverage of big givers [S2]. Participating candidates must disclose every donor publicly in searchable form [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small donors and non-wealthy House candidates

how_it_helps.text: A certified candidate receives a payment equal to 600% of the qualified small-dollar contributions ($1–$200 each) received, with a further payment of up to $500,000 before the general election.
To qualify, a candidate must gather at least 1,000 individual small-dollar contributions totaling at least $50,000 in a 180-day window, showing genuine community support before public money flows.

In three selected pilot states, every resident of voting age would receive a $25 'My Voice Voucher' on request that can be allocated in $5 increments to House candidates, with the FEC reimbursing states' costs up to $10 million per state.

Participating candidates may accept no more than $1,000 from any individual, may spend no more than $50,000 of personal or family funds, and are barred from joint fundraising committees and leadership PACs, shrinking the role of large donors and party money.

The program is funded by a 4.75% surcharge on federal criminal fines, civil and administrative penalties, settlements, and certain tax penalties against organizations and corporate officers; the bill states no taxpayer funds may be deposited in the Freedom From Influence Fund.

analysis.who_pays: Organizations and corporate officers that pay federal fines, civil or administrative penalties, settlements with the government, or certain tax penalties, who would owe an extra 4.75% on top of the amount. Participating candidates give up large-dollar and party funding channels in exchange for public money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations and entities paying federal fines

drawbacks.text: The funding mechanism is a 4.75% surcharge on every federal fine, penalty, and settlement paid by organizations and corporate officers, including certain tax penalties, which raises costs for regulated businesses and passes some of it to consumers; the bill explicitly bars using general taxpayer funds as a backup [S2].
The program would not start until elections in 2030, with FEC regulations due by June 2028, so any effect would be a decade or more from the bill's introduction [S2].

The Freedom From Influence Fund has no guaranteed revenue; if it is short, the FEC must cut payments to candidates and states pro rata and cannot draw from any other source, so candidates' expected funding could fall short [S2].

While candidates receiving public money accept a $1,000 individual-donor cap, the bill allows unlimited coordinated spending by political parties on behalf of participating candidates, so long as it comes from a segregated account funded by small-dollar contributions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully shift how House campaigns are funded: a $50 grassroots donation would generate $300 for the candidate, and self-financed or big-donor-funded opponents would no longer be able to overwhelm participants' totals as easily. The costs are real but targeted—the 4.75% surcharge falls on entities that have already violated federal law or settled with the government—and the no-taxpayer-funds rule, strict fraud provisions, repayment requirements for misused funds, and mandatory GAO reviews are serious guardrails. The main design weaknesses are the delayed 2030 start, the uncertain revenue stream for the fund, and the preserved door for party coordinated spending.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on May 24, 2024 and referred to three House committees—House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means—but none of them ever considered it, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. John Sarbanes introduced the bill on May 24, 2024, joined by Reps. Neguse, Clarke of New York, and Pingree.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Administration Committee and also to the Judiciary and Ways and Means Committees, with jurisdiction to be decided later by the Speaker.
The bill lists 4 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The full action history shows no further steps: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the existing campaign funding system stays in place: candidates who rely on large donors and self-funding, and the industries that pay fines and penalties, are spared the surcharge. Ordinary small donors gained nothing from the bill's death, but they lost nothing either since it had never been in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large donors and the fundraising status quo

for.name: Rep. John Sarbanes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Government by the People Act on May 24, 2024 and sought referral to three committees.

for.name: Reps. Joe Neguse, Yvette Clarke, Chellie Pingree
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All four members attached to the bill were Democrats, and the record shows no Republican sponsor or cosponsor; the bill never reached the stage where votes were recorded.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants and regulated businesses paying federal fines
industries.note: The bill adds a 4.75% surcharge to federal criminal fines, civil and administrative penalties, settlements, and certain tax penalties, which raises the cost of corporate legal exposure. The revenue funds small-donor matching, so the burden falls on entities that already paid penalties rather than general taxpayers.

industries.industry: Political fundraising industry (large-dollar bundlers, joint fundraising committees, leadership PACs)
industries.note: Participating candidates must cap individual donations at $1,000, ban joint fundraising committees and leadership PACs, and spend no more than $50,000 of personal funds, shrinking the market for high-dollar fundraising services. Nonparticipating candidates are unaffected.

Parties lose one route of influence over participating candidates, who must limit contributions to party money subject to existing limits, but the bill also lets national and state party committees make unlimited coordinated general-election expenditures for participating candidates if funded from a segregated small-dollar account.
